voiceover.text: Last time, our research cycle ended on a finding. On national measures, young people are the healthiest age group in Australia. Few die, and chronic disease is rare. So why do health reports keep worrying about them? Before we answer, write down what you think are the three biggest threats to the health of people your age, and next to each one, how you know. A statistic, something a teacher said, something from social media, or a guess.

Death rates alone would say there's little to do. That's wrong, for three reasons. First, the burden is mostly non-fatal. Burden of disease adds years lost to early death to years lived in ill health, and for young people, mental health conditions and injury dominate it. Second, the main causes, like road trauma and self-harm, are events with social causes, not slow diseases, so they're largely preventable. And third, the habits that shape the next sixty years are set now. Young people are low in illness, but high in leverage: what changes now pays off for decades.

The syllabus asks for trends, not levels. A trend is the direction a measure moves across several years, and here, the picture moves both ways. Smoking among young Australians has fallen a long way, one of the country's clearest health successes. Road deaths among young drivers have fallen too. But reported anxiety and psychological distress have risen. That last trend is hard to read, because better recognition and more help-seeking raise reported rates, even if the condition itself hasn't risen as much. Always quote a figure with its source and year, or describe the direction. Look back at your three: how many had a source?

Behind each issue sit two lists. A risk factor raises the chance of a problem. A protective factor lowers the chance, or reduces the harm when the problem happens anyway. They aren't mirror images. Take mental health. Risks include isolation, bullying, family conflict and insecure housing. Protection includes one trusted adult, connection to friends and community, and help-seeking skills. For road injury, inexperience and peer passengers are risks, while graduated licensing and supervised practice protect.

scenes.title: why the protective list is the useful one

voiceover.text: Here's why the protective list matters. You often can't remove a risk, like family conflict or inexperience. But you can usually add a protection. And look at the protective column again. Most of it isn't a decision a young person makes. One trusted adult is a consistent protective factor in adolescent health, and nobody can simply choose to have one. Protective factors are mostly conditions and relationships. That's where the determinants come back in.

Take physical activity, which looks like the purest personal choice there is. Whether a young person is active depends on whether sport is affordable, whether there's somewhere safe and lit to go, whether they can get there without a car, whether paid work fills their afternoons, and whether their family and friends are active. That's five conditions and one decision, and the decision comes last in the chain. Help-seeking works the same way. It depends on whether a service exists, is confidential, can be reached after school, and won't judge you.

So behaviour is where the determinants become visible. It's the last link in the chain, and it's the link people get blamed for. That's why campaigns that only try to persuade young people to choose differently tend to help the already advantaged first, and can widen the gap, just as we saw with the vegetable campaign.

scenes.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people

voiceover.text: The syllabus names Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people, and this needs precision. As we saw earlier, the inequities have historical and structural causes: colonisation, dispossession, the forced removal of children, continuing disadvantage, racism, and services that haven't been culturally safe. They're not explained by culture or by choices. These causes work through the determinants you know, and they cluster, so their effects compound. But describe strengths too. Connection to culture, community and Country protects social and emotional wellbeing, and community-controlled health services are trusted because communities run them. An answer listing only gaps tells a deficit story.
Two things to remember. Young people are low in illness and high in leverage. And the factors that protect them most are conditions and relationships, not decisions.

Two exam questions. First. Someone says, "Teenagers won't go to the doctor about their mental health." Rewrite this statement as a chain of at least three links from a determinant of health to the behaviour, and name one protective factor that would interrupt the chain. Pause here to answer.

One good chain: the nearest youth service is far away and only open in school hours, so getting there means missing class and needing a lift, and a young person worried about being judged puts it off. A protective factor that breaks it is a confidential service open after school, or one trusted adult who helps them go. The classic mistake is leaving it as a choice: they just won't.
Second. Examine the health status of young Australians, referring to trends in key health issues. Pause here to answer.

Open with the paradox: the healthiest age group, yet most of the burden is non-fatal. Name where it sits, mental health and injury, and say it's largely preventable. Then give trends both ways: smoking and young driver deaths down, reported anxiety and distress up. Add the caution that more help-seeking raises reported rates. The classic mistake is telling only one direction, either all good or all crisis.

So, to examine young people's health, start with the paradox, give trends in both directions, pair every risk with its protection, and trace behaviour back to its determinants. Next, we'll take one issue that sits underneath several of these, sleep on school nights, and research it properly.
